questions.prompt: Two assets each have a volatility of 20%, and their correlation is 0.3. You put half your money in each. What is true of the mix's volatility?
options: It is exactly 20%, the average of the two
It is 40%, the sum of the two
It is below 20%, because the two assets do not always move together
It is 0%, because the swings cancel completely
questions.explanation: With a correlation below 1, part of the two assets' swings cancel, so the mix swings less than the average of its parts. Only a correlation of -1 with the right weights could cancel them completely.

questions.prompt: In a covariance matrix for assets A and B, what sits on the diagonal?
options: The expected return of each asset
The covariance of A with B
The correlation of A with B
questions.explanation: The diagonal holds each asset's variance, its covariance with itself. The two places off the diagonal hold the covariance of A with B.

questions.prompt: The optimised weights earn 4.49% at 9.79% volatility, and half each earns 5.00% at 12.04%. Why is the optimised mix still the better choice?
options: It has the higher Sharpe ratio, and leverage can scale it to 12.04% volatility with a higher return
It holds more of asset A, which has the higher expected return
It has no risk at all
questions.explanation: Its Sharpe ratio is 0.46 against 0.42. Scaled up 1.23 times to the same 12.04% volatility, it earns 5.52%, more than the 5.00% of half each.
